Madam Speaker, it has come to my attention through the Hamilton and District Chamber of Commerce that exporters of capital goods in my riding of Hamilton West, like most Canadian exporters, are in

January 26, 1983
serious competition with foreign producers, some of whom offer concessional financing to perspective purchasers. This type of financing is often done with the direct or indirect involvement of the foreign government, which provides interest rate subsidies. In many cases, for Canadian exporters, the difference between obtaining an order or not is the financing terms which they can provide in negotiations with overseas customers.
The Canadian Government has a mechanism by which it can provide financing and support for Canadian export business, namely, the Export Development Corporation. If funds could be made more readily available by the Corporation to Canadian business in order to secure offshore contracts, this would certainly help to stimulate the Canadian economy. With this in mind, Bill C-110, which proposes, among other things, to increase the authorized capital of the EDC from $1 billion to $2 billion, must certainly be viewed as an important step in the process of achieving greater Canadian competitiveness in the export market, and should be given consideration by all parties for rapid passage.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF FARM BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in 1981, 260 farms went bankrupt, and in 1982, 410 farms were forced into bankruptcy. Statistics Canada states that in 1982 farm income dropped 28 per cent from a loss position in 1981. Scores of farms across this nation are on the verge of bankruptcy and thousands of farmers are worried.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), instead of doing something to save our farms, tells the world that "agriculture is in a healthy state". The Minister and the Government of Canada should be taking effective steps, including the following, to help save our farms: Reduce the federal Government's tax on farm fuel which, at 60 cents per gallon, is far too excessive; eliminate the excise tax on gas which, besides other ill effects, is cutting down production because more and more farms cannot afford to fertilize their land; eliminate the capital gains tax so that elderly Canadians may retire in dignity and younger men and women can start farming.
The National Energy Program of the Liberal Government is forcing our farmers to pay a far greater share of taxation than any other group in the country. Saving our farms should have top priority in any economic recovery and should not be left on the backburner, where it is now.

subtopic: EFFECT OF UNITED STATES MEASURES ON CANADIAN EXPORTS
EFFECT OF UNITED STATES MEASURES ON CANADIAN EXPORTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, President Reagan, in his State of the Union Address last night, said that the United States " .. . must remain committed to free trade ..." Perhaps our Government should remind the President that his country's trade practices are not so free as he would have Americans and Canadians believe. A new "buy America" law will act to exclude Canadian concrete and steel firms from U.S. funded highway and bridge projects. One estimate of the dollar loss to Canadian cement firms alone is in the tens of millions.
The United States Department of Agriculture's Blended Credit Program, offering credit guarantees to selected countries buying American wheat, will make it impossible for Canadian wheat producers to export to those countries.
Also of great concern is the future of the Canadian forest industry, and particularly the British Columbia lumber export trade, in light of the current opposition in the United States to our forestry exports to the U.S. I ask our Government to say to President Reagan that his administration cannot " . . . remain committed to free trade ..." until it " .. . becomes committed to free trade ..."

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEPLOYMENT OF PERSHING II MISSILES IN WEST GERMANY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the two super powers are now using the phrase "launch on warning" to describe their response to certain new weapons. The Pershing II missile to be deployed in West Germany late this year is such a weapon. It is extremely accurate and will destroy an enemy missile 1,000 kilometres away in six minutes. The only defence against this weapon is to get your own missile out of the silo before it is destroyed, and the only means, given the short time available is to launch on warning.
What does "launch on warning mean"? There have been, over the past 20 years, many warnings of possible enemy missile launchings, bombers and such, reported by NATO and NORAD. Each has been tracked down and found to be false, so no defensive action occurred. "Launch on warning" means that, since there will be no time to investigate these warnings, a computer malfunction or misinterpretation would result in a launching and trigger a nuclear holocaust.
We Canadians, as members of NATO and NORAD, are part of a process this year which could turn the remote possibility of an accidental nuclear war into one of probability. This House must demand in the name of humanity that the concept and weaponry which could cause a "launch on warning" be forever abolished.
January 26, 1983

subtopic: NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND NEWFOUNDLAND ON OFFSHORE RESOURCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am concerned about the apparent breach of faith in negotiations concerning offshore resources. It is an issue of immense concern to Canada and to the economic life or death of Newfoundland.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) said before Christmas that he was prepared to consider for Newfoundland an agreement on the offshore resources different from that with Nova Scotia. Mr. Marshall of Newfoundland contacted him. They had several meetings and they agreed verbally on certain points of principle which would govern an agreement. The Minister of Energy wanted only a verbal agreement, not an agreement in writing. When the officials sat down to carry out the principles which had been agreed, it was discovered that the federal Government officials did not accept the points of principle on which the Minister had agreed.
There was to be a joint management board of both Governments, for example, with paramountcy in certain areas, but it turned out, according to the federal officials, that all the employees of the board were to be appointed and responsible to the federal Minister.
There are differences between what the Minister agreed to and what his officials say he agreed to. Newfoundland has now telexed the Minister asking him to respond in writing to 17 points of principle. The Minister is refusing to do that. He must do this or be accused of bad faith. Surely it is necessary and reasonable for the points of principle to be agreed upon in writing before officials draft a suggested agreement. Has the Minister of Energy been "hung out to dry" by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde)?

subsubtopic: CALL FOR COMMITTEE STUDY OF REGULATORY AGENCIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the federal Government, under our Constitution, has powers over banks and banking, the use of credit, money supply, and interest. Our forefathers gave the federal Government that responsibility to ensure that Canada would have a sound financial system.
Since this Government came into power three years ago, serious concerns have developed with respect to financial institutions and insurance companies. In the trust field we have had the bankruptcy of Astra Trust and its associated company, Remor. And now we have the defalcations of Seaway, Grey-mac, and Crown. In the insurance field we have had receiverships in Pitts, Strathcona, and Caledonia. Yesterday concern was raised with respect to the Canadian Commercial Bank.
Oral Questions
Clearly there is evidence that the Department of Insurance, the Inspector General of Banks, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Bank of Canada, the Government's agencies that are supposed to be the policemen managing financial institutions, have been asleep. The Government has failed to conduct inspections, failed to follow up on information, failed to act promptly.
Confidence in our financial system is essential. That confidence is damaged by the Seaway, Greymac, and Crown matters, and the concerns reported yesterday with respect to the Canadian Commercial Bank. It is imperative that this House constitute a special committee to examine in detail all of our agencies managing financial institutions to give people renewed confidence.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF FUNDS FOR MUNICIPAL JOB CREATION PROJECTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. In the news this morning the Minister was reported to have said that he agrees with the need for additional stimulus in the economy to provide jobs and specifically, he said, in terms of providing additional infrastructure and municipal works. I point out to the Minister that there is not a municipality from St. John's all the way across Canada to Victoria that does not have at least half a dozen projects ready today that would create jobs throughout the land.
Given the need of more than 1.5 million Canadians to find jobs, and given the presence in municipalities of plans to create jobs, why is the Minister planning to wait another two months, until budget time, to allocate money to provide jobs? Why does he not act now?

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF FUNDS FOR MUNICIPAL JOB CREATION PROJECTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question raised by the Hon. Member was inspired by an excellent meeting 1 had with representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress, and speaking on behalf of two million workers, I am very pleased with the spirit of co-operation shown by the CLC on that occasion. I realize the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party may be somewhat upset about this, but I trust that in the final instance, he will realize it is a development that should be applauded by all Members of this House, and it is to be hoped that labour will work closely with employers and the governments concerned towards the economic recovery this country so urgently needs.
As for the Hon. Member's specific question, 1 shall repeat, if 1 may, what I said yesterday after the meeting, namely, that I have received numerous representations from a variety of organizations which seem to indicate there is a growing consensus that stimulus should be given to investment in the public sector at the municipal, provincial and federal levels, and that consumer spending should also be stimulated. It seems that support for these general measures is very widespread, and I shall, of course, take these representations very seriously because, as 1 said before, they were made by a large number of organizations.
As for what specific decision will be made in this respect, 1 would ask my hon. colleague to wait until the next budget.

Madam Speaker, the Government has not brought forward a new program since October when NEED was announced. From October to the end of March will be five months before we will get a budget. There is some real need, and a feeling of urgency by the people of Canada in respect to obtaining new jobs. The Minister has
Oral Questions
already indicated that the Government is prepared to provide additional stimulus. What is holding him back from announcing it now and saying to municipalities across the land, "Don't wait for another two months; provide some employment right now for Canadians and you will get it from the federal Government"? As a matter of fact the leading economic indicators were all up in the last quarter. Housing has increased for the first time in 16 months. Employment rose in December. There are a number of clear indications that we are on the way to recovery. That expenditure of over $2 billion is going into the economy at the present time.
1 have had a very fruitful meeting with my provincial colleagues, the Ministers of Finance. We have agreed that we will be looking together at everything that could be done at the municipal, provincial and federal levels to help ensure an even stronger recovery. This process is ongoing at the present time. It was made clear at the time, and my provincial colleagues recognized this, that this did not mean the federal Government would be paying for all these activities-that the municipal, provincial and federal Governments had room to borrow and proceed with activities of their own. This is what is taking place at the present time.

They are working hard at this themselves, and municipalities that have projects to go ahead are welcome to go ahead with those projects right now.

PRICE OF NATURAL GAS EXPORTED TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In recent press reports several U.S. Congressmen are claiming success in pressuring the Canadian Government to reduce the price of Canadian gas going into the U.S. market. The Minister has publicly indicated that he is flexible on this subject. His officials will also be visiting Washington on Tuesday to pursue this matter further. Would the Minister
assure the House that he is not prepared to cave in to American pressure to reduce the price of Canadian gas going into the U.S. market?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PRICE OF NATURAL GAS EXPORTED TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the question of price is part of an agreement between the Canadian administration and the American administration which was signed some two or three years ago. The price is $4.94. It has not been increased over the last two years because of the current market conditions.
In terms of the price for future exports, I am waiting for the report of the National Energy Board which is supposed to be published tomorrow in which they will decide if there is surplus and to whom they will give the licence for export. It is only after that that we will have to decide about the price.
At this time the price is part of an agreement between the two Governments. I explained that to the Congressmen, as well as telling them that they cannot blame the increase in the price of natural gas in the United States this winter on a price that was set three years ago and has been in their system for three years.

speechtext: That certainly is not an answer that would give any assurance to provincial Governments that are already having great difficulty with revenue problems.

Madam Speaker, there was an assurance in the National Energy Program to consumers that in order to convert through the off-oil program to natural gas and other alternatives it would maintain gas at 65 per cent of the price of oil. Madam Speaker, the natural gas and gas liquids tax has been set in such a way that the price of gas would be very advantageous to consumers. Our intention, as announced in the National Energy Program update, was to maintain that tax at a level of approximately two-thirds the price of oil in 1982 and 1983.
I am reviewing this matter at the present time and I expect to be able to announce a decision in that regard. I want to assure the Hon. Member, however, that we will reduce the natural gas and gas liquids tax significantly to honour that commitment fully and maintain a very significant advantage in favour of natural gas as compared to oil, as far as consumers are concerned.

East): Madam Speaker, 1 have a question for the Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member will understand that it is not in my power to offer Quebec a stronger veto right in exchange for anything at all. The veto right, if it is recognized for Quebec much as every Province had recognized it in the 1971 agreement, which Quebec rejected, will be a consequence of all Provinces agreeing to the new amending formula. Therefore, I cannot offer any pay-off.
However, I do want to clarify, for the benefit of the House and the Hon. Member, what I wrote in my letter to Mr. Levesque concerning language protection. In essence I was offering to sit down and write a text which would be more protective of minorities, both French and English, across Canada in the educational system. That was the line that the Premier pretended had been adopted at the St. Andrews' meeting in 1977 and the Montreal meeting in 1978 when all Premiers agreed to protect the minority language rights in their Provinces.
It will be recalled that, as the agreement was being reached in November, 1981, I made the same offer at that time to the Premier of Quebec, saying that if the Charter and the particular section concerning language rights did not correspond to the agreement they had reached in St. Andrews and Montreal, I would be prepared to change its wording. But it was not a watering down, as has been suggested by some editorialists, which was indicated in my letter. On the contrary, it was a rewording which I would hope would go even further in respecting the minority language rights.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. The CNR has announced its intention to eliminate 44 jobs in the Mari-times, a move which can hardly be received warmly in a region of the country in which unemployment has already ravaged countless households.
However, the ramifications are much more substantial than 44 lost jobs. In the name of efficiency the port City of Saint John, whose facilities handle more tonnage than any other port on the East Coast, has been reduced to a second class status from a "carload centre" to a "satellite". Will the Minister not recognize the negative impact that this change will have on users and potential businesses in the city, and reinforce the position of the port and the security of the port workers by assuring the city it will not lose its classification as a "carload centre"?

subsubtopic: ELIMINATION OF JOBS IN SAINT JOHN, N.B.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are two answers to questions of that kind, which I receive regularly two or three times a week. One is to emphasize that if we Canadians want our railways to be efficient we have to accept the fact that they have to keep up with improvements, to rationalize, to be efficient. That means, unfortunately, and we all regret it, occasionally the transfer or preretirement or lay-off of some people. That is the first answer. It is a question of knowing what we want and having in mind the real interests of Canadians and of shippers, and trying to develop as efficient a railway transportation system as we can.
The second answer is, and it is a traditional one in Canadian politics, for the Minister to say that we have Crown corporations in Canada and the Minister is not involved in the daily operations of these institutions. That is in line with the best practice throughout Canadian history.

Madam Speaker, the port city of Saint John must remain efficient and it must serve a useful purpose, just as the CNR should be serving it. That city has received body blow after body blow-the cancellation of VIA services, the non-utilization of the port for a fair share of grain movement, to name two recent events-and now this. I will ask the Minister will he not confer with his officials, because he does have an opportunity to influence the CNR, and he should not try to deny that, and ask them at least to postpone the disembowelling of the city of Saint John until
parties at all levels have had some opportunity for input into this decision?

Madam Speaker, I will do so, but I do not accept the proposition which is apparently at the basis of the Hon. Member's question, that the Port of Saint John has not been thriving in recent years. On the contrary.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The Minister is no doubt aware of the controversy surrounding the approval which the Ontario Conservative Government has given to the contract signed between the District General Hospital in Hawkesbury and the Canadian subsidiary of American Medical International which will manage the hospital according to profit criteria, as opposed to health criteria, and of course in return will get a share of whatever profits they can generate.
Does the Minister consider this contract, which sets a serious and dangerous precedent in the privatization and, indeed, the Americanization of health care in Canada, to be in violation of one of the five founding principles of medicare, which is the principle of non-profit administration?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I read the news in the newspapers, like many other parliamentarians, I immediately inquired into the repercussions on the five basic principles upon which medicare is established, and well established. I must immediately, and I am pleased to have a chance to do it in answering the Hon. Member, point out that the Medical Care Act refers to a medical care insurance plan of a province as being administered on a non-profit basis.
According to the legal advice that I have received, medical practitioners or institutions related to health could operate on a profit basis. It is the plan covering the client services that must be administered publicly, not for profit.
I would therefore suggest, before we all panic and think there is something deeply wrong with what Ontario is doing, which by the way is being studied carefully with the purpose of imitating it in other provinces, that we ask the proper question, which is, if that hospital makes a profit, and it is good for the hospital as long as its clients are well served, where will the money go? I think it should increase the services needed in health promotion, for example, and in new work on health concerns. That is where the pressure should be put.

We know where the money will go, Madam Speaker. It will go to the same place where all money generated by multinationals in this country goes; it will go back to

the United States. That is where the money will go, it will not go into health care.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister whether or not she approves of this, not whether or not there is some legalistic distinction between the Medical Care Act and the Hospital and Diagnostic Services Act, which there may well be. What I am asking the Minister is, does she approve of this in principle and, if she does not, will she include something in the next draft of the Canada Health Act to address this problem, because it certainly goes against the spirit of health care in Canada as it is understood by the majority of Canadians.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of providing, in association with the provinces, a scheme whereby the pensions of all employees in Canada who contribute to a pension plan shall be portable from one employer to another without any loss of accrued benefits.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is with great satisfaction and pride that I rise in the House today to present the motion read just now. It was tabled on December 10, 1980. I just want to explain the procedure I had to follow to get this motion before the House today. Madam Speaker, I am particularly proud to be speaking on behalf of over 60 per cent of Canadian workers who do not enjoy the same advantages as their colleagues in the public sector with respect to pension plans, and also the manner in which such plans provide protection for the spouse.
That is therefore why I put this motion, at the request of a number of workers employed in small- and medium-sized businesses who, because they had changed jobs and owing to various circumstances had reached the age of 45 or 44 or 42 without having any kind of pension. During the last election campaign, I promised, and I made a commitment in my parliamentary bulletins to the constituents in my riding of Laval that I would draw the Government's attention to this situation which is penalizing 60 per cent of our workers because they work in the private sector and because they have not had an opportunity to work in the public sector. I therefore put this notice of motion. Several discussions were held in the Liberal caucus among Members from Quebec, Ontario and all the other provinces. In fact, the Liberal Government has been a major force in improving the quality of worklife and developing pension plans in Canada.
As a Member of this party, I could almost rest assured that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Government would demonstrate a firm resolve to take a comprehensive look at the pension plan situation in Canada, and the purpose of my motion today is to propose that for workers in the private sector, pension plans should be portable from employer to employer, until the employee retires.
In view of worker mobility, one aspect of pension plans that should be considered is portability, so that workers will be able to live comfortably upon retirement. In other words, Canadians in the private sector would, upon retirement, have a reasonable chance of avoiding a serious drop in their standard of living.
The purpose of my speech is to ask the Minister to refer this motion to the special committee of the House of Commons, to review the status of pension plans in Canada, and I am thus speaking on behalf of all those workers, men and women, in the private sector who do not enjoy the same protection as do employees in the public sector, at the municipal, provincial and federal levels. In the public sector, pension plans are portable, which means the employee is not penalized if he changes jobs.
January 26, 1983

Private plans financed by the employer represent only 14 per cent of total benefits paid to persons of 65 and over, that is, $1 out of $7, while 60 per cent comes from Government sources, that is, $3 out of $5. At the present time, the most urgent social problem is pension reform, for the simple reason that neither the Canada Pension Plan nor private plans provide an adequate income for Canada's senior citizens.
Today, 53 per cent of 2.3 million retired Canadians have incomes that are low enough to make them eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, which is $194.37 per person for a married couple and $252.10 for a single person. The supplement is added to the monthly $251.12 provided under the universal Old Age Security Program.
This means that one pensioner out of five, or nearly 400,000 Canadians, have no income other than their Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, although they have worked all their lives.
How does the pension system in Canada work? It is often referred to as a three-tiered system. The first level consists of Federal programs including Old Age Security-$251.12 per month-the Guaranteed Income Supplement of $194.37 for a married person and $252.10 for a single individual, and the spousal allowance which is granted to the spouse of a pensioner who is receiving Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, if the spouse is between 60 and 64 years old. Since the Old Age Security Act was amended, about 90,000 pensioners have been receiving these benefits, which represents an annual expenditure of Government funds of approximately $175 million.
At the second level, we have the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans to which contributions are compulsory and linked to earnings, and which apply to practically all Canadian workers between the ages of 18 and 64, unless they are receiving retirement or disability benefits under the Plan.
The third level is the pension plan which comprises private pensions, personal savings and investments which represents approximately 25 per cent.
If we want to ensure the well-being of private sector workers in the years to come, we must treat them as equal partners, and pension plans must be on a level with those in the public sector. It is along these lines that I am going to continue the balance of my speech.
Private pension plans have a number of drawbacks which prevent the elderly from receiving an adequate income upon retirement. Only 40 per cent of Canada's labour force contribute to a private pension plan. There are 380,000 Canadians living solely on Old Age Security and Guaranteed Income Supplement benefits, despite the fact that they have worked for a number of years. This problem must be solved first of all, because even if we do change the rules on portability, it would not do much good if 60 per cent of our workers were not able to benefit.
Transfer of Employee's Pensions
A number of arrangements regarding vested rights leave much to be desired. The employee is entitled to his pension plan contributions as soon as the employer's share becomes the employee's property. A number of companies require a long period of service-as much as ten years-and the recipient must be 45, before they agree to pay the employee what he invested in the pension fund as soon as he turns 65. An employee who leaves a job and does not have ten years of service with the same company, loses the employer's share. The employer returns the employee's share, keeps his own, and the employee may receive interest of up to 4 per cent. The result is that all these workers are penalized because pension funds are not portable. Sometimes workers reach the age of forty without having any pension plan whatsoever.
If we look at figures provided by Statistics Canada, we see that in 1976, only 10 per cent of contributors to private plans were eligible to receive the full amount contributed to their pension plans. In view of the very considerable mobility of Canadian workers, people who change jobs have no protection at all as far as pension funds are concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I am not setting myself up as an actuary or an expert on the subject, but I believe that as a Member of Parliament I have a responsibility, with my fellow Members, to try and correct this unfortunate situation which is penalizing men and women working in the private sector and I believe we have a duty to ensure they have at least the same level of protection afforded to public sector employees. That is the purpose of my motion, and I realize that eventually a price will have to be paid, and that the Government, in addition to "recharging the batteries" of our Canadian economy and safeguarding and creating jobs, will also have to continue its efforts in the area of pension reform and consider my notice of motion as one of its priorities. I appreciate the Minister's concern for the predicament of spouses who are not protected in the private sector, as our legislation now stands.
I am well aware of the rules of this House, and I do not intend to use up all my time. I wish to appeal to all parties to make this notice of motion more than just an earnest wish expressed by a Member of this House on behalf of 60 per cent of the working men and women of Canada, and to have this motion referred to the special committee announced in the House by a Government that is indeed making a tremendous effort to improve the status of pensioners in Canada. On December 9 last year, we tabled in the House a document entitled: "Better Pensions for Canadians", and we also announced the formation of a special committee. I should therefore appreciate it if this notice of motion were referred to the committee.

subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO ESTABLISH TRANSFER SYSTEM WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to express my appreciation to the Hon. Member for giving us an opportunity to debate the merits of this particular motion.

January 26, 1983
Transfer of Employee's Pensions
The need for greater probability of private pension schemes is obvious to most Members of this House, particularly in a period of high unemployment. There are literally thousands of individual workers who have paid in to private pension plans and are now suddenly faced with, and affected by, plant shutdowns. Because they do not have a particular number of years of service and a vested interest in a private pension plan, they suddenly find that the pension they thought they had bought is in fact not there at all. Very often all they are entitled to is the return of contributions, and even that at a very low rate of interest; sometimes it is something less than 4.5 per cent based on the contributions they have made to that particular plan.
While all workers, male and female, are affected detrimentally by that kind of situation, for women it presents a different kind of problem. The reasons for that have been stated by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), who has pointed out on a number of occasions that simply because of the position of women in society and the workforce, they tend to change their jobs about six times during their work life. That being the case, it becomes increasingly difficult for many of those women to build up a pension benefit through the private pension plan system. And not only that, very often it is impossible for many women in the workforce to earn a pension benefit on retirement because of the inequalities and inequities built into our workforce structure.
The mover of this motion, when he wound up his speech, Mr. Speaker, referred to the green paper on pension reform which was recently tabled in the House by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. As the Hon. Member knows- but it may come as a surprise to the House-that green paper dealt primarily with reforms to the private pension system. When I asked the Minister a question about what was going to happen to that green paper, she made it absolutely clear that the thrust of the green paper and the statements it contained- they were not even recommendations-were related directly to the private pension system.
Now, while I would be the first to agree that there will always be a place in our retirement income structure for private pension plans for those individuals who wished to buy an additional benefit over what public plans provide, I think it is an abdication of this Government's responsibility to place the total thrust of any policy development to improve retirement incomes on the private system. I say that for a number of reasons. First of all, the private plans cover less than 50 per cent of the workforce, and out of that number of people only about 33 per cent are women. At the National Pensions Conference held here in Ottawa several years ago there was absolutely no doubt in the mind of anyone who participated that the private pension system is totally inadequate for the needs of people who retire today. In fact, there has hardly been a newspaper editorial since that green paper was tabled, and for some time prior to that, which has not emphasized that if there is any kind of policy development on reforming our pension system, it should be weighted in favour of the public
plans, particularly the Canada Pension Plan. The reasons for that are obvious.
The Hon. Member's motion is welcome in terms of allowing the House to debate the merits of this particular proposal to improve portability from one private pension plan to another. 1 want to point out, however, that the best kind of portability is already provided for in the Canada Pension Plan. It is completely portable. If you are laid off at one plant and then become employed at another, the Canada Pension Plan is still there; your contributions are still there, the benefits you bought are still there and it is guaranteed to be paid to you at retirement age. In my view, that is the best kind of portability that can be provided. It does not demand a certain level of income to allow you to buy an additional benefit, as would be necessary under a private pension plan. In my view and that of many other people, the Canada Pension Plan is probably much more desirable than any improvement in the private system which would provide a benefit to the largest number of people in the country.
There are obviously other problems which many Members on this side of the House addressed in the debate on Bill C-131 which took place in the House in the last several months. We pointed out repeatedly that the benefits provided under the Old Age Security Act are totally inadequate. That statement is justified when it is recognized that the vast majority of single women over the age of 65 have annual incomes of something less than $5,000 per year under the Old Age Security Act. I challenge any Member of the House and most Canadians to try and scrape by on that.
While we are talking about improved portability provisions within private pension plans, I think we would be remiss in our responsibilities if we did not address these other serious problems that are built into the income replacement system for retirement that we have in this country.
A number of groups and individuals have been concerned with the plight of retired Canadians and those who have not had an opportunity to buy into a private pension plan over the years. One such group is the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto which, on December 10, 1982, issued a statement that addressed the particular problems faced by single, elderly people. It said, in part:
On average, unmarried elderly persons in Ontario who are supported only by government income guarantees are currently living over $1,300 below federal poverty lines. In large urban centres, such as Toronto, Ottawa or Hamilton, such persons have incomes which are nearly $2,000 below the poverty line. The Social Planning Council estimates that a minimum adequate income for unmarried elderly persons in Ontario is about $350 a year more than the poverty lines in 1982. These elderly persons cannot wait until after the much delayed process of pension reform reaches parliament in 1984 or later ...
While pension reform for those who have not yet retired is urgently needed, the needs of those who have already retired, particularly elderly persons who live alone, is much more urgent. The current debate on pension reform will not help the poor elderly person, because few have any pension benefits in the first place.
That is a matter that should be of serious concern to anyone who has any sensitivity or recognizes that there should be a form of social and economic justice in the country.
January 26, 1983

At a recent conference held by the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, the whole question of pension requirements was addressed. The research director, Louis Erlichman, stated as follows:
Resolving the pension issue is becoming increasingly urgent as the number of needy elderly Canadians grows.
Statistics Canada figures show there now are two million Canadians over 65 and more than half of them are living on less than $6,000 a year.
The federal agency's figures also show that once the baby boom generation of the 1950s starts to retire, the number of over-65s will more than triple.
Meanwhile, about 43 per cent of the country's population has no investment or private pension income.
A discussion on the need for complete portability between the pension plans in the private system is welcome, but 1 think we have to extend the discussion to requirements in the public pension system as well.
I want to thank the Hon. Member for giving us this opportunity to address this particularly serious question today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join with the previous speaker in thanking the Hon. Member for Laval (Mr. Roy) for bringing this matter to the attention of the House. I believe it is important because it is an issue that will be with us for a long, long time. As the previous speaker indicated, it is a problem for a growing number of elderly people in the country.
When one looks at what we have come to call the post-war baby boom bubble moving through society-I presume they are now in their thirties and forties-one can see that the issue is not just one of immediacy for people now aged 65 and over, but that it will be exaggerated enormously when the baby boom bubble moves into retirement in the next two or three decades.
As I understood the remarks of the Hon. Member for Laval, the principal thrust was that the committee consider the nature of this motion as part of its mandate when it studies the broader issues. To that I enthusiastically and whole-heartedly subscribe. For the last ten years I have believed that the greatest underutilized force of this Chamber is our committee system. I hope that the parliamentary reform proposals will do something to correct that. I have some serious reservations, however, about the genuineness of certain Members of Cabinet in terms of fulfilling that potential for committees, but I hope I am wrong. As we move into a rather changed committee system, I have great hopes for improvement.
I cannot think of any subject-although I am sure there are some-that would provide a better subject matter for intensive study than the whole issue of pensions. I sincerely hope the issue of portability will become one of the major issues that the committee will study.
The Hon. Member for Laval professed that he was neither an accountant nor an expert on pensions. I do not think that is very important from a committee point of view, Mr. Speaker. As a bachelor, I am sure the Hon. Member was not an expert on wife battering, yet he chaired the committee that studied the subject and which, I say in all sincerity, was one of the
Transfer of Employee's Pensions
greatest stimulants in society. In my riding, an active committee of volunteers was created as a direct result of the committee and it is now working on the problem.
The Hon. Member need not make any apologies to the House for not being an expert on pensions or for not being an accountant, because were that performance to be repeated by the committee studying pensions and a report drafted that would have as much success and progress and make as much impact as the one on battered wives, then the Hon. Member would have made a very significant contribution not only to the House but to society.
Let us talk a bit about the problem of pensioners. I claim not to be unique at all, but I come from a riding in which the principal employer for many decades was the CNR. One of the great attractions of working for the CNR, as many of us will remember, was its pension plan. By comparison, in the 1940s and early 1950s its pension plan was very attractive. As a result, CNR pensioners in my riding and dozens of others across the country looked forward to a reasonable retirement in their own homes. That pension plan, as many others, has become a victim of inflation. The pension has been so seriously eroded by the ravages of inflation that the reasonable expectations of these pensioners have not been met.
I should like to direct my remarks particularly to portability.
I agree that women have been the principal victims of pension plans or the lack of viable pension plans. If one looks at typical young persons in the work force served by private pension plans and acknowledges the mobility of workers, not only geographically but from one employer to another, one finds that many of them upon changing jobs regard for good reason the contributions they have made to the pension plan of their previous employer, together with any interest which has built up, as a sort of savings. Suddenly it becomes-and 1 hate to use the word-a windfall gain when they have their previous employer that may be used to purchase a car, to take a holiday or to pay debts, which would be more likely in today's society. In my view, it is because of lack of portability that they have been regarded as temporary savings plans rather than as plans for future retirement.
If we can do anything to encourage a change in attitude toward that contribution, we should do so. We should work in the House and in the committee toward changing the attitude among young people in the work force who regard it simply as a supplementary savings plan to be cashed in when they change jobs. Their attitude should be changed to regarding it as something to supplement the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security.
The Hon. Member pointed out a number of people were receiving GIS. This is directly attributable to the fact that people have become either discouraged or uncaring during their working years about supplementing income for retirement years or creating additional income for retirement years. Certainly portability is one of the best tools available to us toward changing that attitude and experience. Therefore, I

January 26, 1983
Transfer of Employee's Pensions
hope the Government consider, as a result of the Elon. Member s motion, that the portability factor be one of the major items to be studied by the committee.
1 hope I do not imply something incorrectly in the motion. In part it reads:
-the Government should consider the advisability of providing, in association with the Provinces, a scheme whereby the pensions of all employees in Canada who contribute to a pension plan shall be portable from one employer to another without any loss of accrued benefits.
1 do not believe the Hon. Member is suggesting that we exclude private carriers or that the Government pension plan should supplant all private plans. He is suggesting, rather, that the Government should take some action, in consultation with private carriers, to encourage portability of private plans. I see him nodding in the affirmative. I very much support that concept.
I was somewhat disturbed by the spokesman for the New Democratic Party. I think he intimated that the Government should be the exclusive carrier of pension plans. That was not the intention of the Hon. Member for Laval. Again I thank him very much for bringing the matter before the House of Commons in this form. I wish him great success in convincing his ministerial colleagues that the substance of this motion should be included in the terms of reference for what I hope will be a very successful committee study.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO ESTABLISH TRANSFER SYSTEM WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks by commending the Hon. Member for Laval (Mr. Roy) for his very timely and very fine reminder of the importance of this issue. At the end of his comments he mentioned the pressing need to look at the economy and that he did not want to divert us from that issue. I assure him that the issue of pensions deserves our attention at this stage and that it will not divert us from other economic topics. We are indebted to the Hon. Member for his timely reminder and for the ideas he put forth.
1 know that in his work as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs he has constantly shown a concern over this matter. I know as well that he raised these comments in correspondence and in our caucus meetings. He has travelled about his own riding gathering evidence and commenting with his constituents.
Today's discussion moves the issue one step further. We are all the beneficiaries of this and we thank him for it. They are important ideas which deserve our attention now. Some of them deserve our immediate action.
1 should like to refer the Hon. Member to some comments which were made before the Finance Committee during its special hearings in September. At that time we looked at the Income Tax Act and our discussions touched upon quite a few points, including the problems in terms of pensions, especially equity issues for farmers, small-businessmen and professionals who need to take a capital asset and turn it into a pension. We discussed how they could do that without suffering undue tax burdens. There was a very useful discussion of the problem at the time. The Hon. Member may want to take a look at it as a smaller issue inside the one which he raised.
We all have observations which we want to make on the topic. Personally, I am struck by the importance of home ownership for many Canadians. Very often home ownership gives retired Canadians a great degree of security, a kind of security which is not apparent when we look at the otherwise low incomes they enjoy. For example, one of my neighbours is a widow who is in her eighties. She owns her own home and takes advantage of public sector pensions. She is able to live in that manner because she does not have a heavy burden in terms of shelter costs; she is able to enjoy her own home.
1 wonder whether we should be exploring further the question of using RRSPs for home ownership, given the obvious evidence that Canadians are able to live at home and not rely too much upon outside pensions; they are able to get by with what otherwise seems to be minimal incomes. I know there are some tax issues involved with that proposal. It is an old idea; it does not originate with me. It seems to me that we should be able to overcome the tax-related problems of immediate benefit, of creating an undue tax shelter and so on. We should be able to work out some kind of compromise between the tax issues and the needs of Canadians in that respect.
Last December, as the Hon. Member knows, the Government presented its green paper on pension reform. I want to talk about some of the issues on pensions that come from the Finance Department. I know my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Schroder), has some other comments that he wants to raise from that department s point of view. From the Finance Department s perspective, we published a paper on pension reform that we thought set out an important array of proposals and some issues involved in upgrading our private sector pensions and our income support system. At the same time, I think it has been proposed that a special parliamentary committee be formed that will submit a report by the end of 1983.
I think the idea which the Hon. Member for Laval has raised should be directed to that committee, which should be asked to react to these very important insights.
January 26, 1983

The portability of private pension plans has long been a concern of the Government of Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other Ministers have promised that pension plan credits will be made more portable than they are now. These initial studies that we have undertaken are the first steps along the line.
The difficulties created by the existing limitations on pension portability are well known. The Hon. Member for Laval raised some and so did Members on the other side. One problem is that belonging to an employer-sponsored pension plan does not necessarily mean that employees will ultimately receive a pension at retirement. They lose their pension rights if they change employers or if they lose their jobs before retirement.
While such employees may have their own pension plan contributions returned in such circumstances, they frequently forfeit the benefits that would result from the contributions made by their employers. I heard the ideas put forth by the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis). I thought it important that we look for some way and some incentive to keep younger people involved in pension plans rather than simply encouraging them to spend the money right away. I know we found similar problems with young employees who regard health and dental plans as unnecessary expenses, for example. They do not see the sense in these kinds of plans in their stage of life. We might want to take a look at that idea to see if there is some incentive that can be built into the system to follow up on the Hon. Member's ideas.
Many workers end up in their retirement years either with low pension benefits or none at all, even though they may have worked most or all of their working lives with various employers who offered pension plans.
In Canada the problems involved in portability of pension benefits are exacerbated by the high labour mobility that exists here. We have estimates that a male worker can hold jobs with as many as six employers during his working years. The average female worker may expect to have even more than six different employers during her working life. On the one hand, this mobility is a very healthy sign, both for the individual and for the economy. For the individual it means greater opportunity to switch employers rather than to progress slowly up the ladder in the same company. For the economy, there is a great deal more productivity coming from these people and many more benefits because of the greater use of their skills and knowledge. But the limitations to pension portability are creating a real barrier to job mobility for many Canadians. It becomes a disincentive for them to switch employers, to seek better opportunities and to make more productive use of their skills.
Therefore, in the green paper we find, as just one of several of its considerations, a whole series of proposals aimed at promoting high mobility through greater portability of pension rights.
First, we have to consider the question of the vesting of an employee's rights to pension plan contributions made by the employer. This is naturally an issue that is very closely related
Transfer of Employee's Pensions
to pension portability. The Government believes that vesting provisions, that is, the time or age at which an employee is entitled to receive a pension credit based on the employer's contribution, must be substantially improved. The green paper proposes that vesting occur after two years of service. Otherwise, improved portability provisions would in many cases merely have the result of transferring the credits resulting from the employee's own contributions.
In respect of portability itself, the green paper has suggested that three options should be available to an employee when he leaves a job after his pension rights are vested. Subject to adjustments related to the funded status of the pension plan, the employee could have the following three choices. First, the employee could transfer the entire value of the pension to a registered pension account. This would be a new retirement savings plan, and I will elaborate further on that in a few minutes.
As a second option, the employee could leave the accumulated credits in the former employer's plan and take a deferred pension when he or she reaches normal retirement age.
Another option would be a combination of the two I have just mentioned. The value of the employee s contributions, with interest, would be transferred to a registered pension account while he or she would take a partial, deferred pension by leaving the remainder of the value in the plan with the original employer if the employer agreed. Or the employee could transfer the value of the accumulated pension to a new plan with the new employer, if that new employer agreed. Alternatively, amounts that could be transferred to a registered pension account could instead be transferred to a pension plan with the new employer.
How does this proposed new approach compare with the current provisions under pension law and income tax rules? The present legal framework generally allows employees to transfer the value of their vested pension benefits, tax free, to another pension plan or to a Registered Retirement Savings Plan, provided certain conditions are met. However, pension plans are not required by law to provide for such transfers.
In practice, we find a variety of approaches to this question. In the public sector many employers have reciprocal agreements among themselves to transfer credits for pensionable service when an employee moves from one such employer to another.
In the private sector the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association has sponsored a somewhat similar arrangement among some of its member companies. A few industries, such as construction and forestry, have some multi-employer pension plans. However, in practice the majority of private industry pension plans do not provide for the transfer of vested benefits.
There are a number of other issues which have a bearing on the portability of pension rights. For example, most private plans do not provide for automatic indexation of benefits to maintain the purchasing power of pension rights in the face of inflation. Until such indexation becomes more prevalent, many

January 26, 1983
Transfer of Employee's Pensions
employees might be better off if they simply took the cash on leaving an employer and invested it in such flexible instruments as Registered Retirement Savings Plans which could remain constant with inflation as the years go by.
This situation has led the Government to bring forward, as a proposal for consideration, the idea of requiring a minimum degree of inflation protection. This is the so-called excess earning method. Under this method, adjustments would be based on the difference between the five-year average of Government of Canada long-term bonds and 3.5 per cent. This proposal clearly has long-reaching implications and there must be broad consultations with the private sector and provincial Governments before it can be implemented.
I spoke earlier of the proposal in the green paper for a new retirement savings vehicle, the registered pension account. This would operate in a rather similar fashion to a Registered Retirement Savings Plan except that employers would also be able to contribute to an employee's registered pension account on a tax-deductible basis.
The proposal for a registered pension account has the potential of providing a very simple but effective way of improving pension portability. The details of such a plan are currently being developed within the Government and it is intended to publish a discussion paper on the whole question within several months. It should, however, be an important part of public discussion and debate which the Government hopes will take place on the whole question of pension reform.
Naturally, provincial Governments will have to be involved. They will play a key role. As the Hon. Member for Laval indicates in his motion, the Provinces have an important input in any decision on pension portability. The Provinces are responsible for regulating 90 per cent of workers and their pension plans in Canada. Over the years the federal and provincial Governments have co-operated closely in building a pension system that is substantially uniform throughout the country. In this way we have established and maintained Canada-wide standards, encouraged labour mobility and minimized administrative burdens for our employers. Federal-provincial co-operation will be more important in tackling the next stages of pension reform.
One point that I am trying to make in these remarks is that pension portability is important but it is not the only issue that must be considered as we attempt to achieve reform in our pension systems. There are other important matters that I have not mentioned which have to be carefully examined. There are questions of broader pension coverage for our working population and questions of improving pension treatment for women. We must ask ourselves, for example, what kind of balance we should strive for in seeking better retirement income protection between employer-sponsored pension plans, the more broad-based contributory Canada Pension Plan and Quebec pension plan, and the universal Old Age Security system.
It is noteworthy, for instance, that in the last several years there has been little or no increase in the proportion of workers covered by employer-sponsored pension plans. The percentage of employed paid workers in such plans increased from 42 per cent in 1970 to 47.9 per cent in 1979, but dropped marginally to 47.7 per cent in 1980. We must also ask ourselves how much pension reform can be afforded. It may in fact be necessary to choose among the elements of reform if they cannot all be afforded at once.
The green paper on pension reform examines all these wider issues. It contains proposals to improve the Canada Pension Plan and strengthen Government support for the elderly with low incomes. It also discusses issues related to financing the Canada Pension Plan.
The green paper proposes that a special parliamentary committee be set up to examine all of these proposals and to submit its report by the end of 1983. I hope that it will be possible to proceed at an early date with this committee study. I wish the committee well and at the same time I want to recommend to the committee the thoughtful presentation which we heard today from the Hon. Member for Laval. I want to thank him for raising these issues again and providing a chance to discuss them once again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO ESTABLISH TRANSFER SYSTEM WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the short time that I have available I would like to say that I know my Minister would consider the subject of pension portability, the subject of this motion today, to be well within the mandate of the special committee on pension reform. I am sure she will be anxious to have the subject referred to this committee and that it be given open and full discussion by the special committee on pension reform.
I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on this motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Laval (Mr. Roy). I commend him for bringing this motion forward, as it contains the elements of a solution to one of the main problems with Canada's pension system. Indeed, I am certain that the reason or rationale behind the motion must be immediately apparent to anyone who has been following the pension debate in Canada over the last several years. Of course, I am speaking of the problems caused by the lack of suitable vesting and portability provisions in private pension plans.
As a result of the interaction of these two factors, vesting and portability, few workers in Canada who have had at least some degree of coverage under a private pension plan during their careers reach retirement age with any significant amount of income from this source. The only people in Canada today who are likely to receive an adequate pension from a private pension plan are those who have not only paid into the pension plan but have been working for the same employer for all or most of their working years. Far too few Canadians fall into this group. This is a very strong factor which contributes to the inadequacy of pensions today.
The obvious solution to this problem is contained in this motion. Let all employees in Canada take accrued benefits
January 26, 1983

with them when they change employers. Of course, the problem in fact becomes less simple under detailed examination. That is why the problem remains with us. However, that is not to say that it is insoluble, nor that it has been ignored by Governments in the past. Indeed, as a direct result of Government action, there are two contributory pension plans in Canada at this very moment which achieve everything which could be provided as a result of this motion. I am sure Hon. Members are aware that I am speaking of the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. Hon. Members will recall that one of the main forces, if not the force, behind the introduction of these plans was the need to solve the problem caused by a lack of transferability of an employee's accrued benefits from employer to employer.
How did the introduction of these two compulsory, contributory social insurance schemes deal with the problem of portability of accrued pension rights? The answer lies in several key elements of these two plans. First, membership is compulsory for virtually all workers in Canada between the ages of 18 and 65 as long as annual income is above a certain basic amount. This means that every worker in Canada is covered by one of these two plans, regardless of their length of service with the employer, the size of the company, the industry they work in or even the number of hours they work in a week. Unfortunately, all of these factors can affect the employee's coverage under an employer-sponsored pension plan at any given point in time.
The second key element is that all pension credits attributed to any one contributor to the Canada or Quebec Pension Plan are immediately vested.

that Bill C-317, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code (Safety

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to introduce Bill C-317, a private Members' Bill to amend the Canada Labour Code. The purpose of the Bill is to amend the Canada Labour Code to make the provisions of Part IV, relating to the safety of employees, applicable to all federal work undertakings, including the operations of trains, ships and aircraft, departmental corporations and private and local works in the Territories.
I would first of all like to make it clear that I do not suggest that this Bill will solve the problems of health safety facing the workers of Canada. This Bill will deal with a few of the problems but, more important, I hope we can use the debate to convince the Government of the need for major changes in health and safety legislation. I shoulld not have to work hard to do this because it is not a partisan issue. The Minister has admitted in speeches that we lose more time through injuries than through strikes.
The Conservative labour critic has spoken often on this subject, and the NDP conducted a task force which travelled right across Canada and saw at first hand the problems that workers face in the workplace each day. It is a very, very serious problem.
Mr. Speaker, we all agree on the size of the problem. According to Workmen's Compensation Board figures, there were over a million work injuries in 1978. In the ten years before that the size of the work force had risen by 29 per cent and the number of injuries had risen by 69 per cent. Under the Canada Labour Code, one in every eight workers suffered a work injury or was killed in 1978. The same figure was true for workers in federal Crown corporations. On top of that, the Department of Labour admits that these figures may underestimate the problem by as much as 20 per cent. It is quite possible that there are a much larger number of injuries than even these figures report.
There is a great deal which could be done to reduce these injuries. In the first place the Labour Department does not have enough inspectors. Back in 1978 there was an article in the old Labour Gazette which contained a comment that is as true today as it was then. That article said that the main problem was:
A system which put the inspectorate in the front line of the battle for occupational health and safety, in insufficient numbers, with confused and inadequate battle orders and a poor supply of armaments.
Less than a year ago we discussed this whole question for an estimates committee. We found at that time that there were 13,200 work sites under federal jurisdiction. There were 8,000 new work sites added, with the addition of the post office, under the Canada Labour Code. To inspect those 20,000 work

develop. This has to cause us all great anxiety, especially since one-third of all cancer deaths are said to be occupationally related.
1 would like to quote from a report on the hazards concerning the reproductive system at work. The President of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, Lucie Pepin, said:
We have found that almost all workplaces contain hazards to the reproductive system; not only factories, nuclear plants or mines, but also hospitals, offices and schools. These hazards do not simply harm pregnant women, but other women, men and future generations as well.
It is a very serious problem. In spite of that fact, we have no federal law enforcing disclosure of chemicals in the work place and the Provinces do not have the power to do it.
I would like briefly to speak on the right of workers to police the safety of their own environment. The Government told us it would give workers this right in 1978, when it introduced amendments creating health and safety committees and allowing the right to refuse dangerous work. However, the health and safety committee were not mandatory. In 1981 only 700 such committees were in place on our 20,000 federal job sites and, of those 700, only about 50 had been imposed by the Minister. The difference between a voluntary committee and an imposed committee is that the imposed committee has a great deal more power. That is why many employers will try to get the unions or workers to agree to a weak voluntary committee. Once again, the former Minister of Labour had admitted he was disappointed at the small number of committees which had been formed, but even those committees have few rights.
The right to refuse dangerous work is based on imminent danger. In other words, if a truck is about to fall on someone, it is immiment danger. However, if someone were dying by degrees from chemicals in the air, there is nothing that one could do.
The state of health and safety laws at the federal level is awful. They are also the worst in Canada. The NDP knows this, as does the Official Opposition. Certainly Canadian workers know it, and even the Government knows it. For two years the Government has been sitting on recommendations which would bring about needed improvements, such as making committees mandatory and improving the right to refuse dangerous work. The legislation is written. I asked the Government to present it and perhaps save some lives.
The annual cost because of health and safety problems is nearly $4 billion. Surely that kind of saving is more important than the money saved by cutting Public Service pensions. Surely the loss and ruin of lives of Canadian workers should be our first, not our last, priority.
Finally, I ask the Government to go further and give the Department of Labour the kind of funding it needs to carry out its mandate. Within its existing mandate and funding, surely the best thing it could do to improve the quality of the working life would be to remove the danger of loss of workers' lives.
The Bill I have presented today deals with one aspect of the problem I have raised, the problem of other Government legislation having more power than the safety and health
Canada Labour Code
provisions of the Canada Labour Code. 1 hope by raising these other matters that I might encourage the Government to act on them as well.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) for raising this matter in the House this afternoon. The opening remark of the Hon. Member, when he said that the issue of health and safety was not a partisan one, was appropriate, and I think all Members of the House share his concern for the safety and security of public servants of Canada.
In rising to speak on Bill C-317, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code, I would like to refer to the explanatory note which gives us insight as to the purpose of the Bill. The note states:
The purpose of this bill is to amend the Canada Labour Code to make the provisions of Part IV relating to safety of employees applicable to all federal undertakings, including the operation of trains, ships and aircraft, departmental corporations and private and local works in the territories.
As Your Honour knows, Part IV of the Canada Labour Code sets out a range of minimum standards to be used by employers to protect the safety and health of their employees. Employees who are within federal jurisdiction are in such enterprises as banks, broadcasting, airlines, shipping, railways, interprovincial trucking, telephones, and other undertakings which have been deemed to have been for the general advantage of Canada. As things stand at the moment, federal public servants do not come within the purview of the Canada Labour Code and I think the Hon. Member was quite right in his research on this question. Their safety and health are protected by the provisions of the Treasury Board policy and standards which are indeed similar to the requirements of Part IV of the Code.
The occupational safety portion of the Treasury Board's program is handled in a similar manner by Labour Canada, but Health and Welfare Canada administers the occupational health portions of the program. The objective of these regulations is, of course, to ensure that work is respectful of human life. The law also underlines the general principle that all Canadians have the right to a healthy and safe work environment regardless of the jurisdiction.
Another point I wish to bring to the attention of Hon. Members is that Part IV of the Labour Code does not apply to employment involving the actual operation of ships, trains or aircraft. Bill C-317 does have definite merit. I am pleased to inform Hon. Members that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) has been holding extensive consultations with representatives of labour, industry and other federal Departments in order to prepare a comprehensive revision proposal for Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. These discussions are proceeding, and I anticipate that an amendment proposal to the Canada Labour Code will be introduced in the House in the very near future. Any proposed changes to the application of the Code must, however, accommodate situations where international laws, agreements, public safety, and a concern for passenger

January 26, 1983
Canada Labour Code
safety in the transportation field take precedence over the "safety of employees" provisions included in Part IV of the Code.
Bill C-317 is, however, in my opinion, slightly regressive in one area, that is to say, where the Bill proposes that the undertakings or business of a local or private nature within the Yukon or the Northwest Territories should revert to federal jurisdiction. This recommendation, in my view, is contrary to current practice and can only be seen as a sorry step backwards to what is supposed to be an orderly evolution in the development of the Territorial Government.
Although several aspects of Bill C-317 are commendable, the Bill should be considered in the context of the development of a more comprehensive amendment to Part IV of the Code. This process must involve extensive consultations, which we believe are currently under way, to develop an amendment proposal which considers all aspects of a contemporary occupational safety and health legislative program.
I have not taken much of the time of the House, but I wanted to put those comments on the record. I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for presenting this Bill. I know how interested he is in this matter. I have had the privilege of working with him in committee. He is preoccupied with the safety and health standards of this country. I want to congratulate him, and I hope that this Bill is accepted.

Mr. Speaker,
I wish to say a few words on Bill C-317, which is an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code, (safety of employees). The Hon. Member who introduced the Bill has asked that trains, ships and aircraft, departmental corporations and private and local works be included in Section 80 of the Canada Labour Code, Part IV, dated May, 1981. It states that ships, aircraft and trains are to be excluded from this section of the Act. I do not know how that came about because I was not involved in the drafting of this particular piece of legislation, but if the Minister is going to bring in changes and improvements to the Labour Code, I believe we can make some inquiries in committee as to why trains and ships have been excluded in Section 80 of the Canadian Labour Code.
We, of course, are all concerned with the health and safety of all workers, whether they are in a mine or a factory, in an office, or even in the home. It is interesting to read some facts and figures which indicate there are more accidents in the home than in any other location, and a lot of this is caused, for example, by a person using an unsafe ladder or standing on the edge of the table, or what have you.
I notice the Ontario Government uses television extensively to get the safety message across, and 1 think that has been most effective because actual demonstrations are given of just how accidents happen. I hope they continue with that kind of exposure and that the day will come when they will expand into areas other than the industrial area. In order to have proper safety practices, Mr. Speaker, management training is
very important. If a manager does not understand the rules of safety and cannot explain and train his staff in the importance of the rules of safety, for example, the use of hard hats, safety glasses and safety shoes, then he is not much of a manager and he will not have much of a safety record with his crew.
I was a foreman in industry for many years and I took a great interest in safety. I found that proper training will eventually get the message across, but it is difficult. A lot of people want to take a lot of shortcuts. They do not want to examine their ladders. They do not want to wear a hard hat or to wear safety shoes. It is difficult to get the message across to some people on the importance of safety.
I found it very rewarding over the years as the majority of my crew eventually caught on to the art of safety inspections of their equipment, and it certainly pays off in the long run. There are a lot of excellent films available across Canada on the subject of proper safety procedures, and I used these safety films extensively. There have been great advancements in safety equipment as well. Perhaps one of the most prominent pieces of safety equipment is the hard hat. Everyone who works on new building construction sites or renovation sites is wearing a hard hat, so the message has certainly been put across in regard to wearing hard hats on construction sites.
The Hon. Member who introduced the Bill spoke extensively of problems in mines. I agree with him that there could be a lot of improvements made in that area. If you are 500 or 600 feet below the ground, you certainly do not want any risks to be taken. We certainly want the most up-to-date safety equipment for anyone working in a mine.
I am looking forward to the changes which the Minister is going to be bringing forward, and I am sure the Hon. Member who introduced the Bill will be present at the committee meetings. We will have also representatives from the Conservative Party at the committee to review carefully the new recommendations which will be coming from the Minister. I believe his Parliamentary Secretary is here today and perhaps he will enlighten us further on what changes the Minister will be bringing forward.
