speakeroldname: Mr. Antonio Yanakis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments on the statement made by the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) concerning Bill C-137, An Act to amend the Canada Labour Code (safety of employees) Part IV. As I understand it Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to extend the scope of Part IV dealing with employee safety to all employees coming under federal jurisdiction, including employees of the Public Service of Canada and of private and local companies operating in the Territories.
I think that it would be worthwhile to provide this House with a brief background of Part IX of the Canada Labour Code and point out some technicalities contained in other orders. The Canada Labour Code is a digest of various federal
January 26, 1983

measures dealing with labour issues. It sets out some standards for workers in the private sector who come under federal jurisdiction. Part IV of the Canada Labour Code deals with health and security at the workplace and includes statutory provisions provided under the act and setting forth minimum standards which employers must enforce in order to ensure the security and health of their employees.
Even if Part IV of the Labour Code is the only federal legislation which deals exclusively with those issues, it does not apply to all workers in the private sector coming under federal jurisdiction.
That situation, Mr. Speaker, stems from restrictions related to the application of Part IV of the Code. Because of such restrictions, any other Act of the Parliament of Canada and its regulations take precedence over Part IV, the provisions of which do not apply to persons employed on ships, trains or aircraft, including their operation, unless the Governor in Council has issued an Order in Council stating otherwise. Part IV excludes as well any undertaking which is defined as a department or a corporation under the terms of the Financial Administration Act. In accordance with recent amendments to Part IV of the Canada Labour Code, employees now have the right to refuse to work under conditions which, in their opinion, constitute an immediate danger to their safety or their health. In addition, as a result of the proclamation of provisions giving them the right to create health and safety committees made up of employer-employee representatives, workers now take a more active part in the operations of the company, except, as I just said, those who work on ships, trains and aircraft.
Mr. Speaker, the laws dealing mainly with public safety on the safe operation of various means of transportation overrides the Labour Code provisions concerned with safety and health. The health and safety in the workplace of employees subject to those acts are looked after by departments and agencies whose primary responsibilities and expertise are not related to those areas.
Those departments enforce laws that deal with a specific sector, namely railways, and look after their safe operation and the safety of the public.
During the early discussions on the Canada Labour Code (Safety), it was clearly established that the Code would only complement existing federal laws and would only apply in those instances where those laws contained no similar provision on safety and health in the workplace.
At the time, Mr. Speaker, labour organizations had strongly recommended that the Code should apply to all employees coming under federal jurisdiction. Since 1966, they have taken that stand on several occasions. Yet, it was decided that the purpose of the legislation, which was to guarantee the safety and health of all workers, could be achieved by enforcing the Code only in those instances where no such protection was
Canada Labour Code
provided under existing legislation. In the last several years, there has been far more concern for the health and safety hazards in the workplace. Due to the work-related diseases suffered by some of their members, unions have become more aware of those hazards and a good number of them are now giving top priority to safety and health problems.
Many western industrialized countries have now recognized the need for regulatory agencies to deal better with health and safety problems and have therefore increased the number and the quality of their programs to ensure safety and health in the workplace, mainly by combining all regulatory agencies into a single agency. Thus, Mr. Speaker, when it endorsed the recommendations of the Roben Commission, the commission inquiring into health and safety in the United Kingdom felt that the separation of legislation from its administration was causing a scattering and a compartmentalization of the technical facilities and knowledge available across the country to fight occupational hazards.
Mr. Speaker, occupational safety and health problems vary from one industry to the next, but the Commission felt that many had technical characteristics in common and required the use of similar professional and technical knowledge.
During the same period, the U.S. government was facing similar problems. Following discussions within the government the Occupational Safety and Health Authority was set up to administer the Occupational Safety and Health Act (1970), which includes many acts which until then came under various agencies.
In Canada, the provinces are taking similar steps to do away with the fragmentation of legislation in this respect. However, as far as Federal jurisdiction is concerned, it is often impossible to act quickly and efficiently to protect the health and safety of a large number of workers, because responsibility is spread over a large number of departments where there is a definite lack of co-ordination of activities. Many workers covered by other parts of the Canada Labour Code are not covered by Part IV.
Mr. Speaker, it is sometimes said that work-related hazards come under two clearly defined headings: health and safety. Experts on prevention agree that when they want to determine causes and set up preventive measures, the two concepts are so closely linked that it would be unthinkable to consider them separately. Mr. Speaker, that is why most national bodies in industrialized countries have set up health branches that are solely concerned with occupational health. The branch reports to a central, regulatory body that is responsible for occupational health and safety in all sectors.
This division was created in accordance with the recommendations of the board of directors of ILO, according to whom occupational health and safety cannot be considered separately and must therefore be dealt with as being part of the same problem.

January 26, 1983
Canada Labour Code
Mr. Speaker, more recently, Commissioner James Ham stated in his Report of the Royal Commission on the Health and Safety of Workers in Mines, Ontario, 1976, that certain cases of occupational stress affected both health and safety. Dealing separately with health and safety as far as workers are concerned constitutes another false dichotomy, maintained by company policies and regulations.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see that the technical resources of Labour Canada, including the support required for investigations as well as an analysis laboratory, have been expanded so that now most of the hazards occurring in the occupational environment, both in the public and private sector, can be dealt with. With these new facilities and the full time services of a specialist in industrial medicine Labour Canada has been able to improve its work safety and health services.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly support the principle of this bill which concerns employee safety. Guaranteeing the safety of workers is not only a matter of interest, but a major concern for the Minister of Labour and the Government. Because of this, the Minister of Labour has undertaken a series of major consultations with interested groups with a view to developing a cohesive set of amendments to the Canada Labour Code. Of course, this includes the principles of the bill now before us. Mr. Speaker, I believe that these amendments should be reviewed as a whole rather than in isolation. I believe that the Government wants to introduce all these amendments at the same time to the House in the near future. This is why, Mr. Speaker, I would recommend that this bill not be supported in its present form.

Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed the address of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Yanakis) until the last sentence. I cannot follow his line of thought. This Bill is not partisan; it has nothing to do with political Parties. The whole object of the Bill is to prevent accidents and to extend the provisions of the Canada Labour Code.
I want to commend the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) for bringing the Bill forward. I hope the Government will take a positive view of it because it does not affect one political Party more than another, it is to the credit of any political Party to try to prevent accidents in this country, and the broader we make the provisions of the Canada Labour Code, the better it will be for everyone. The object is to prevent accidents.
The Parliamentary Secretary stated that the Minister was going to introduce amendments, and of course that would be an excellent thing. What better way of doing it, though, than by canvassing the ideas of a parliamentary committee on this and on other amendments? If this matter were referred to a parliamentary committee, it could do all the work and the Code would be better as a result, as more minds would be
directed toward its improvement. If Hon. Members opposite have not made up their minds already that they are not going to support the Bill, I suggest it would be a feather in their hats if they were to send it to committee. This would be in the interests of the safety of workers in this country, but to talk the Bill out on second reading would be a disgraceful thing. I urge Members of the Government to think positively about this matter.
If this were a Bill that affected one political Party more than another I could understand Members of the Government talking it out, but I cannot understand their talking out a Bill that is intended to prevent accidents and make the workplace safer for our workers.
1 intend to complete my remarks and sit down, Mr. Speaker, so that the Bill will not be talked out, but there are two points that I should like to make.
I do not think we are making enough use of workers' and employers' safety committees today. In the coal mines I have found that for many years employers have resisted safety committees, but after experience with them, employers found that the committees reduced the cost of compensation and reduced the pain and agony suffered by employees as accidents were prevented. The safety committee was composed of workers who knew the conditions in the coal mines; we should make greater use of their knowledge regarding safety.
Most of the safety inspections of working conditions are inadequate. There are not enough inspectors. There should be better inspection, particularly where intricate machinery is involved. It sometimes happens that machines are left exposed and, as a result, a worker loses a hand or a foot or some other part of the anatomy. These matters could be discussed in committee, and the Canada Labour Code could be improved as a result.
I urge Members of the Government to send the Bill to committee, not to be prejudiced and negative and talk it out. It would be to their credit to refer the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of assisting the Government in talking this Bill out, either. I want to commend the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) for presenting it to the House. I cannot think of anything that is of greater importance to working people than the proposals it contains. In fact, it is the kind of measure that the Government should have introduced a long time ago, instead of waiting for a Member of the Opposition to do so.
As the Hon. Member pointed out, the sensationalism caused by man hours lost due to strikes in the country is always brought to the public's attention. It should be realized, however, that in each of the last 12 years, more man hours have been lost due to industrial illness and injury than were lost due to strikes or labour disputes.
That fact does not seem to be generally known but it demonstrates the need for the kind of amendment that the Hon. Member has proposed today. I think it would be to the shame
January 26, 1983

of the Government if its Members were to talk the Bill out rather than refer it to the committee for action.

Mr. Speaker, 1 also should like to commend the Hon. Member for presenting this Bill, and I agree in principle with what he proposes to do. At the same time, I must say that I disagree with some of the comments of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). I had the impression that he had not even listened to the speech of the Parliamentary Secretary who said that the Government wanted to do more than the Bill sets out to achieve and has not decided to put aside its objective of extending the application of the Canada Labour Code.
It is easy to blame the Government for filibustering something or for blocking legislation proposed by a private Member. One should recognize, however, that when a piece of legislation is not complete in itself, it should be examined in that perspective. I did not hear the two Members of the NDP who spoke make a point about the implications of this Bill for the Northwest Territories and their autonomy. Nor did they say anything about the matter mentioned by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) concerning the effect of modifying, without examining the impact, the application of the Canada Labour Code to labour organizations or Government corporations that are subject to international law. These are things worth looking at when we deal with this kind of legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I must say however once again that I am in agreement with my colleagues who congratulated the Hon. Member for Kootenay-East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) for introducing Bill C-317, which aims at extending the provisions of Part IV of the Canada Labour Code relations to the safety of employees.
Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members will know that the Canada Labour Code combines several federal statutes establishing standards for private sector employees who come under federal jurisdiction. Part IV of the Code deals with the safety and health of employees and set out a range of minimum standards to be used by employers to protect the safety and health of their employees. However, Part IV does not apply to all private sector workers under federal jurisdiction, and this is precisely the situation that the Hon. Member wants to remedy. In principle, I agree with him on this point.
Moreover, as stated in the existing legislation, Part IV of the Labour Code does not apply to sea, rail and air workers. Hon. Members would probably be interested to hear that, in the federal government, nine major departments or agencies administer 16 different statutes dealing in various degrees with work safety and health. This is one problem. These government departments are the Departments of Labour, National Health and Welfare, Agriculture, Environment, Indian and Northern Affairs and Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The Hon. Member has made a suggestion and I am certain that
Canada Labour Code
today's debate will give us a better understanding of the problem and will make it possible for the government to take all necessary action to improve the situation.

Most of the 16 statutes to which I have referred were enacted to regulate particular industries such as the railways, to ensure the safety of their operations and the protection of the public. It was piecemeal legislation developed over the years. In all of them, occupational safety and health is incidental to their main purpose. It was because of this that the original Canada Labour (Safety) Code, which later became Part IV of the consolidated Canada Labour Code, was enacted by Parliament in 1966.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-317 now before us is to extend the application of Part IV of the Act and not to increase the number of inspectors as the Hon. Member from Bow River (Mr. Taylor) mentioned. The administration of the Act would remain unchanged but Part IV of the Canada Labour Code would apply to all federal workers. As I said earlier, this is a very commendable purpose insofar as it will provide better and more comprehensive safety and health protection for federal employees. I do not intend to vote against the principle of this bill even though some of its provisions should be amended.

For example-and I referred to this in my opening remarks-the territorial exclusion provided in Subsection 80(1) would need to be retained. To take the right to regulate works, undertakings or businesses of a local or private nature away from the Governments of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories would not only be unjustified at this time but would run counter to the steady development of Territorial Governments and autonomy.
The proposed Bill would also extend the coverage in Part IV to include federal public servants. In this respect I would point out that in the federal Public service, with the Treasury Board acting as employer, the Government several years ago affirmed the policy of applying the principles of the Canada Labour (Safety) Code and the regulations and standards adopted thereunder to the Public Service. I do not know why we have to send the Bill to committee so quickly since the Government is applying these at this moment.
The portion of the proposal which would make departmental corporations subject to the Canada Labour Code has merit, but a case is still being developed to demonstrate that adequate occupational safety and health protection for federal public servants can best be achieved under the provisions of Part IV of the Code itself, not in an application clause.

Mr. Speaker, I understand from what my colleague the Parliamentary Secretary said earlier, that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia), in conjunction with other ministers, has

January 26, 1983
Continental Shelf
been holding consultations for several months in order to develop a safer environment at the workplace and to update the Labour Code so as to provide a better protection for workers in today's High-tech world.

Since the Minister has been consulting to achieve a better Labour Code which would be more adapted to the 1980s and 1990s, I do not think we should accuse Hon. Members of the House of not being interested in the safety of Canadian workers in general or of those who fall under federal jurisdiction. Hon. Members should understand that our main objective is not to have the House make a quick decision. We want to take the necessary time and wait for a few weeks for the Hon. Minister to come forward with a complete proposal to revise the Code so that it will meet the approval of labour organizations themselves.
Although we support the intent of the Bill, with the exception of the Territorial reference, we do not believe it should be considered until a complete package of code amendments is developed following a consultative process with labour, industry and other federal Departments. I do not think I can recommend to the House at this time the passage of the Bill on second reading.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, too often Opposition Members have blamed us for our inefficiency and incomplete legislation. We have been told many times there is a lack of planning in our policies. Well, given the fact that a Minister of Labour has finally undertaken a complete review of the Canadian Labour Code, especially Part IV which prescribes security and health measures concerning employees under federal jurisdiction, it seems to me that we should commend the Minister and thank him for not relying on ad hoc volitions. We are duty bound to help him introduce soon a bill which will be debated, and which, hopefully with the support of the whole House, will achieve the goals pursued by the Hon. Member.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-373, an Act respecting the continental shelf be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to extend Canadian jurisdiction of the sea to the extremities of the continental shelf for the purpose of conservation, protection and management of marine resources. It is interesting to note
that this Bill speaks to the length of this record session because it received first reading on May 2, 1980. One might suggest that it has been overtaken by events in that since May, 1980, Canada has signed the Law of the Sea Treaty. However, 1 intend to establish arguments that this Bill is just as relevant today as it was when it received first reading several years ago. I can anticipate the argument of the Government, especially that of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). Likely it will be that foreign nations during the course of discussions leading up to the Law of the Sea Treaty have made it very clear that they have very strong views against any further extension by Canada of our 200 mile limit. I accept that. However, it is equally true that the countries with which we enjoy bilateral fisheries relations, our partners in the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, recognize our special interests beyond 200.
I believe the case can be made, just as the case was made for our unilateral move to declare jurisdiction within 200, to extend our jurisdiction for purposes of managment, if not for the continental shelf then at least for those two areas known as the nose and tail of the Bank. This is an area of the Grand Bank which is currently outside of the 200 mile limit. I think we can make that case the same way by getting support and agreement from our partners within the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization. They would recognize our right to manage stock beyond 200 on the nose and tail of the Bank just as they recognized our right in the bilateral agreements leading up to the extension of our jurisdiction to manage the area within 200. This makes sense because fish know no boundaries. We are talking about transboundary stock when we talk about the area of the Grand Bank known under the old 1CNAF system as 3NO, DLN, 3-0 and 3LNO.
I remember one of the first things I had to do upon assuming the responsibilities of the portfolio of fisheries was to close this particular area of the Grand Bank to further fishing of cod because the stocks were so depleted at that time.
However, we have been very successful in rebuilding the stocks within our jurisdiction under the 200 mile limit, but we have not been successful in the management of this particular stock because we do not enjoy the exclusive right to do so. That situation is complicated by the fact that the most offending nation is Spain. Spain has, for its own reasons, elected to stay outside of the NAFO convention. It is not part of the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization, and does not come under NAFO management. If Spain does not come under NAFO management and it does not come under Canadian management, then Spain is beyond control, and that is the problem.
To give you an idea of the importance of that stock, Mr. Speaker, the average groundfish catch on the Grand Bank, the 3NO and the 3LN area is 124,000 tonnes, broken down into
25,000	tonnes of cod; 32,000 tonnes of redfish, and the balance in various species of flounder. The problem we are facing with Spain choosing to remain outside of NAFO and our own
January 26, 1983

inability to extend our own management regime is that Spain is depleting stock by the persistent use of a technique known as pair trawling. What the Spaniards do in that particular area known as the tail of the Bank is to have two trawlers that trawl together and sweep up everything. Our own experience based on experimental fishing indicates that with that kind of pair fishing one gets 50 per cent cod with the balance by-catch being flounder. The Spaniards are not interested in flounder or flatfish, or whatever you want to call them; they are only interested in the cod which they salt and take back to Spain to dry. By and large, the flounder is thrown over the side. It is lost. It is destroyed. That has impacted directly on the plants situated along the south coast of Newfoundland which depend to a large extent on this stock. These plants have established markets for flounder. What the experience has been year after year as this situation continues out of control is that the size of the flounder keeps getting smaller and smaller because the stock is not managed.
I know that I would be out of order if I were to refer to the Kirby Task Force which was supposed to have reported in November, then again in December. It is now almost the end of January and the Kirby Task Force still has not reported, Mr. Speaker. But the reason I mention the Kirby Task Force is to inject into my remarks the seriousness of the situation in terms of the Atlantic fishery which is currently on hold, having gone through perhaps the worst crisis in its history awaiting the results of the Kirby Task Force. I realize that the Kirby report will not address itself to this particular problem. I realize that while it is a special interest problem for the Department of Fisheries, it is the specific responsibility of the Department of External Affairs, regardless of what Kirby recommends, to address itself to the problems of plants that are currently down especially along the south coast of Newfoundland. Unless we get this situation under control all of the recommendations in the world will not address the basic problem resulting from the fact that Canada does not enjoy total management of this stock.
I do not want to take up too much time so that other Hon. Members will have a chance to participate in this debate. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) will be addressing some remarks to the Law of the Sea. It is important to remember that we are not talking about the seabed, fossil fuels or seabed mining. We are concerned with the management of the marine resources and Spain's failure to comply with international conventions or to recognize Canada's right to manage this stock.
The record will show that Spain has been harvesting the major bulk of this stock over the years, thereby representing a prima facie case. We have made attempts to come to grips with the Spanish situation. There is a current offer being considered in which I believe we have offered 5,000 tonnes of groundfish in our zone in exchange for access of a limited amount of our fish in the Spanish market, with the understanding that they would be good boys and play the game. That deal has not materialized as yet and, quite frankly, I call it blackmail. Even if that deal is consummated-which I hope
Continental Shelf
never happens-the Spaniards will still not adhere to an adequate management regime. This is because they answer to no one and are not subject to inspection either by NAFO or Canada. They are totally on their own and totally out of control.
There was an interesting report published by the Economic Council of Canada last year which was entitled "The Promise of Abundance: Extended Fisheries Jurisdiction and the Newfoundland Economy". They had this to say at page 61 about the Spanish situation, including by-catches which I have referred to. It reads:
It is much to be hoped that Spanish-Canadian relations will improve in the future, both so that the management of 3NO cod as a transboundary stock will be improved, and so that the aforementioned co-operative arrangements can, at a minimum, be explored. It would be unfortunate, to say the very least, if both opportunities were lost to Canada.
These opportunities are lost to Canada. Our experience with Spain on bilateral agreements has not been a happy one. We must get tough with the Spaniards.
I believe that if we were to pursue this with our partners within the North Atlantic Fisheries Orgnization, we would receive their support in extending our jurisdiction beyond 200, at least to take in the area known as the nose and tail of the Bank. If this does not occur, we will never have control of the management of that stock and we will continue to be faced with a situation where we do not control the by-catch and have no access in terms of inspection of what happens out there.
It is indeed worth mentioning that one of the suggestions made by the Economic Council of Canada was that Spain be allowed to land its cod catch in Canada in return for agreeing to conservation and Canadian management. Of course that would give us an opportunity to acquire the very expensive bycatch, the majority of which is flounder, that is currently being dumped over the side. I might add that this is seriously affecting the flounder stock which, in turn, is adversely affecting the plants and operators on the south coast of Newfoundland.
I hope that Hon. Members will agree with the arguments that I have presented. It is not an unreasonable proposition and one that would be supported by our fishing partners. I believe that it would enjoy support within NAFO since I do not think Spain has any intention of signing the NAFO convention. While there is a suggestion that Spain may eventually join the European Economic Community and thereby become part of the NAFO agreement, we still have to deal with the Spanish problem until that time comes. Unless we deal with it in a direct and effective way, unless we get tough with the Spaniards, we may have to close that very important traditional fishery, which again is so important not only to the fishermen of Newfoundland but to the fishermen of Nova Scotia.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-373. I note from the explanatory note that the purpose of this Bill is to extend Canadian jurisdiction of the sea to the extremities of the continental shelf for the purposes of the

January 26, 1983
Continental Shelf
conservation, protection and management of marine resources. Without doubt, this is a most commendable objective. I congratulate the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) for bringing it forward. There is no question that it is a timely matter and one which must be properly dealt with. The Hon. Member has made some very powerful arguments for its immediate consideration. He has mentioned the Grand Bank. I suggest that it has always been understood throughout Canadian history that the Grand Bank belongs to Canada in their entirety. I do not believe anyone would question that fact. The Hon. Member also stated his concern about the pair-trawling that takes place, particularly by the Spanish fishermen. He also talked about the resulting wastage of flounder that occurs. I wish to commend the Hon. Member for bringing these issues to light.
On January 1, 1977, Canada established a 200 mile fishing zone. This was done following many years of careful preparation and a host of bilateral and multilateral negotiations.
Prior to the extension of jurisdiction in 1977, Canada negotiated bilateral agreements with, inter alia, France, Norway, the Soviet Union and Spain. I suggest it is noteworthy to see that Spain was included at that time, prior to the extension of the jurisdiction in 1977. These agreements anticipated and cleared the way for the establishment of the 200 mile zone. Multilaterally, Canada was one of the handful of countries chiefly responsible for bringing about a consensus on the 200 mile fisheries limit at the United Nations Law of the Sea Conference. This consensus-I stress consensus-on fisheries jurisdiction helps to transform customary international law and enables countries like Canada to adopt the 200 mile limit without provoking chaos and conflict with other countries.
While working to advance Canadian Fisheries interests at the Law of the Sea Conference, Canada was also pursuing regional initiatives to the same end, in particular through the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries. Beginning in 1972, we obtained through the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries steadily growing recognition of the coastal states' preferential rights to the harvest of fisheries resources off their shores. In 1975, we obtained, once again through this international commission, a 40 per cent reduction in foreign fishing effort in 1976 for groundfish, as well as a reduction in the total allowable catches for depleted stocks and higher quotas for Canadian fishermen for stocks of particular importance to them. In 1976, we obtained, once again through the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries, a further reduction for 1977 in total allowable catches that we considered necessary, together with estimated allocations for Canadian Fishermen generally corresponding to their harvesting capacity. In effect, this amounted to recognition of extended Canadian fisheries jurisdiction even before this extension had taken place.
Furthermore, in the closing weeks of 1976, Canada secured an agreement on amendments to the International Commission for Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Convention that restricted the Commission's management authority to the area beyond national fisheries limits, and left management within 200 miles
to the authority of the coastal state, while also leaving Canada with the right to board and inspect foreign vessels beyond the 200 mile limit under the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries' scheme of joint international enforcement.
The efforts made by Canada and other countries in bilateral and multilateral forums created the conditions essential for the extension of Canadian jurisdiction: the extension was consistent with international law and had won international political acceptance.
We in Canada are neither boy scouts nor superpowers. We could not impose our will on others by force, even if we believed it were proper to do so. Nor are we among the countries of the world that can pretend to play David out to slay Goliath, hoping that sympathy for the little guy can win our battle for us. We were able to enforce our jurisdictional claims because they were accepted by other countries. It would have been much more difficult to impose them if other countries had been determined to resist.
Had Canada acted in defiance of international law, then not only would it have become much more difficult to enforce Canadian law and regulations within the areas of claimed jurisdiction, but Canada would have been less able to rely on international law in order to safeguard its other interests as well, including those in the fisheries sector.
Canada relies on international treaties, generally accepted principles of international law and international co-operation in order to protect, for example, its valuable salmon fisheries. This is of particular importance on the West Coast where, in the words of the report of the Commission on Canadian Pacific Fisheries Policy, presented in September, 1982, it said:
-the five species of Pacific salmon are by far our most important fishery resource in both quantity and quality.
If the Canadian PaciFic salmon Fishery were open to unrestricted foreign high seas fisheries it would provide for fewer benefits to Canadians than it does today. It is international law and international co-operation which prevents that situation from arising. International law and co-operation are also of importance to Canada's East Coast salmon Fishery. It beneFits from provisions of Canada's fishery treaty with the European Community as well as the provisions of the Atlantic salmon convention.
We also rely on international law and international cooperation in order to protect Canada's fishing interests with respect to our continental shelf fish stocks, some 10 per cent of which are outside our jurisdiction. Canadian concerns here are addressed in part by the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Agreement. It is, however, essential that we continue to obtain the co-operation of other countries to ensure the proper conservation and management of these outside stocks and appropriate allocations for Canadian fishermen.
The last example I will cite of a fisheries resource that requires international co-operation if it is to be protected, is
January 26, 1983

halibut, a straddling stock. The halibut fishery is among the oldest on the Pacific Coast. The fishery began in the nineteenth century off the coast of Washington State, and significant Canadian participation began during World War I.
Landings by Canadian and U.S. fishermen peaked in the 1920s, at some 70 million pounds, then declined to about 30 million pounds in the 1930s. Recognizing the need for cooperation, Canada and the United States included a halibut treaty in 1923. 1 might digress at this moment to say that the 1923 treaty marked the importance of a milestone in Canadian history because it was the first international treaty that Canada signed in its own right and not by the United Kingdom acting on Canada's behalf. The conservation programs established pursuant to the treaty were successful in rehabilitating the stocks so that landings rose to 75 million pounds in 1962. The halibut treaty was revised in 1979 and is still in force and makes a significant contribution to the productivity of the stock.
Bill C-373 seeks to address the question of outside stocks mentioned a moment ago. It, however, would seek to govern those stocks without any international political or legal support. Such a claim to jurisdiction would be very difficult to enforce, if adopted, and would harm the initiatives that Canada has taken to protect Canadian fisheries interests. For the long term, it would likely undermine the international cooperation that is necessary to protect those stocks not already fully protected by the establishment of the 200 mile zone.
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for bringing forward this very timely matter, which is just as timely today as it will be tomorrow and in the foreseeable future. I commend him once again for keeping this in mind because the more we have control over and the better we manage the Grand Banks and other areas, including the continental shelf, the better it is for Canada and all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to also speak on Bill C-373 today, and I would note that, as the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) said, this Bill was introduced for first reading in 1980.
I think it is reflective of the lack of ability of the federal Government to deal with the Grand Bank, and particularly the Flemish Cap-the nose and tail of the Grank Bank-that we still find this Bill is as pertinent today as it was in 1980, and it is reflective of another failure of the fishing industry off the East Coast, that is, the agreement which failed between the United States and Canada on Georges Bank and the very valuable fishery in that area, in particular the very valuable scallop fishery.
So we have a situation again where, for the purposes of conservation, to say nothing of the implications for employment and foreign exchange in those fisheries, we have a Government which has failed to come to some international agreement with a nation which, granted, has had a long history of fishing off the Grand Bank, and that is Spain. But the problem still exists that our stocks on the Grand Bank beyond 200 miles are indeed being threatened by overfishing, just as
Continental Shelf
the stocks within 200 miles have been threatened by overfishing in the past.
We have been able to demonstrate in Canada that given the opportunity to manage stocks, we can foresee a revival of fish stocks on the Grand Bank and off our East Coast in general.
Nevertheless, despite the agreements under the Law of the Sea-and I think we all recognize that there are some tremendous benefits to Canada from the Law of the Sea and from the signing of that treaty earlier this year in Jamaica-we are still faced with a situation where we really do not have control over some of the fish that are transboundary fish. They do not know what the 200 mile limit is and obviously the federal Government has not been able, either through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans or, more particularly, through the Department of External Affairs, to come to a suitable agreement with Spain, just as they failed to come to suitable agreements with the United States with respect to Georges Bank.
To the credit of the Canadian fishermen, they are not prepared to enter into a fishing war off Georges Bank with their counterparts in the United States, despite losing hundreds of millions of dollars of revenue, because the U.S. fishermen and the United States administration, and in particular the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, sees fit to allow their fishermen, the scallop fishermen in particular, to break any international understanding, even if was not an agreement, finally signed.
I think this Bill is timely. I think it should go to the Fisheries and Forestry Committee for further study. I think it would indicate to the Spanish Government the commitment of the House of Commons that we come to an agreement on stocks that are being exploited and which are damaging employment opportunities, not only here in Canada, but which will certainly in future affect employment in Spain both of fishermen and onshore workers.
The situation in the fishing industry in Newfoundland, as many of us know, is very critical. Communities in Newfoundland are losing their fish processing plants, particularly in Burin and on the Grand Bank. There is a great deal of doubt whether those fish plants will continue in operation. The employment situation in the Province of Newfoundland is deplorable, as it is in most Provinces. So I see a great deal of merit in sending this Bill to committee and for the committee to study the implications that the Hon. Member for St. John's East pointed out.
However, when we are discussing marine resources beyond the 200 mile limit, I think we can also study the mechanisms within the limit to protect and conserve marine resources. There is certainly some question involving protection of our fisheries in Atlantic Canada from pollution caused by offshore oil exploration. We know that when Bill C-148 was being discussed in the House and in committee, we really did not have any input from the Minister of the Environment (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
January 26, 1983
Continental Shelf
Roberts) or the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane), two Ministers who should have been more prominent in the discussion of offshore exploration for natural gas and oil. Certainly, if Canada ever gets to the point where it starts further exploration of other mineral resources on the East or West Coast, this Bill would give opportunity to the Members of the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to assess more accurately our capabilities of managing, conserving and protecting marine resources within the existing 200 mile limit.
Therefore, speaking on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I think the Bill has merit. We would certainly like to see it referred to the committee and would give our support and congratulations to the Hon. Member for St. John's East for presenting the Bill as far back as 1980.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to say a few words about this Private Members' Bill, Bill C-373. I note that it was given first reading on May 2, 1980, when the Law of the Sea Convention was in the process of being negotiated. On December 8 and 9 of last year, if I remember correctly, the Law of the Sea Convention was signed in Montego Bay, Jamaica, by a number of countries. That did not make it international law. It will become effective upon the deposition of the ratification instruments by 60 nations. Canada did sign, of course. One of the interesting things is that Spain did not, its objection to this particular convention being matters concerning international straits. Obviously, it had Gibraltar in mind. Incidentally, as I hope to show before my allotted time has expired, there is another matter which we should be able to persuade Spain to accept which would resolve this very delicate matter in terms of the existence of the flounder stocks off the coast of Newfoundland, off the Grand Banks.
The matter at issue concerns the extension of the very extensive provisions respecting "conservation, protection and management" of the living marine resources beyond the 200 mile limit, where Canada already has very extensive jurisdiction.
The territorial sea concept is a very particular one dealing with the first 12 miles from the baselines off our coast. There we are not solely concerned with marine resources, although they are there too. The clauses of the treaty mainly deal with the passage of vessels, military and otherwise, free traffic including submarines and the over-flight. However, the text of this particular Bill deals with the territorial sea and its extension out of the edge of the continental shelf for purposes of the conservation, protection and management of marine resources. It has been clearly stated that marine resources means the living marine resources of the sea. The Hon. Member for St. John's East very carefully and fully explained the matter at issue. The extension involves hundreds of square miles, not thousands of square miles. It is a small portion. The graphic illustration on page 16 of the document to which he made reference, entitled "A Promise of Abundance", published in 1980 by the Economic Council of Canada, shows just what amount of territory is involved.
An effort ought to be made to secure co-operation from all those members of the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization in order to preserve the stocks for them and for the rest of mankind. Canada has a responsibility in that exclusive economic zone, as well as privileges, and its responsibility is to care for the stocks of fish which are to be found there and breed there. Its responsibility is to establsh that amount of fish which can be taken without destroying stocks. This small portion just beyond the limits is recognized in the Law of the Sea over which Canada does not have jurisdiction.
Flounders, as I remember correctly, are groundfish. They sit on the bottom of the sea, and that is certainly part of the problem. They are scooped up by draggers from the bottom of the sea inside the elusive economic zone. If they are destroyed in their breeding time, they will cease to be an economic resource for Canada or any other country, even those who fish and throw their catches over the side because they do not want them.
It is interesting to consider the provisions of the Law of the Sea Convention. Article 76, for example, defines the continental shelf. We are discussing the edge of the continental shelf at the moment. It defines the continental shelf of a coastal state as extending "beyond its territorial sea throughout the natural prolongation of its land territory to the outer edge of the continental margin". This is a very good illustration. It states that the "coastal state shall establish the outer edge of the continental margin" wherever it extends beyond the 200 nautical miles in a manner which fixes "points which are not more than 60 nautical miles from the foot of the continental slope". That is a very clear definition of how far out this Bill seeks to extend Canada's jurisdiction.
Canada's jurisdiction is undisputed and will be undisputed when the Law of the Sea Convention is ratified and becomes operative throughout the world. By the anomaly of geology, I suppose, the plate on which Newfoundland sits, the Grand Banks, extends just beyond those 200 miles.
For those Hon. Members who are wedded to metric I might suggest that 200 miles refers to 200 nautical miles, 240 statute miles or 370 kilometres. That is the breadth of the sea over which Canada has jurisdiction and can make arrangements with foreign fishermen to fish within that area on the basis of quotas. And that is basically-and I am over-simplifying perhaps-one of the things which the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization purports to do within that area and beyond. There is a general agreement out in the North Atlantic that fisheries will be managed, but one particular country has so far refrained from becoming a member of that Organization, as we have heard described.
The Law of the Sea Convention extends a number of powers to the coastal states, which they may exercise out to the edge of that shelf. On the East Coast the edge, as we have already seen, extends beyond the 200 miles. We have also seen how that extension is defined within the terms of the Law of the Sea Convention. Canada, having signed the Law of the Sea
January 26, 1983

Convention in Jamaica last month, 1 am sure will abide by its provisions. Within that 200 mile limit, which is known in the Law of the Sea Convention as the "exclusive economic zone", Canada, as the coastal state, exercises, as its name implies, exclusive economic powers limited only as prescribed in the Convention, relating to innocent passage, as I mentioned, over-flight and other matters relating to commercial navigation.
For present purposes, however, in this Bill we are considering only conservation, protection and management of living resources, and those rights already exist in the Convention within that exclusive economic zone. Those extra hundreds of square miles beyond were described, I believe, as the "nose and tail". I would describe it from this picture as the nose and chin, even, because it is almost a human face here, but I will accept the nose and tail description of the Grand Bank, those few square miles. It should be no great problem, I should think within the context of the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization, and bilateral agreement to have that extension worked out.
What are the exclusive economic sovereign rights of Canada within that area? Article 56 of the Law of the Sea Convention makes it quite clear what the coastal states can do and to what extent its sovereign rights are exercisable. Those sovereign rights exist for exploiting, conserving and managing the natural resources, living or non-living, of the waters superjacent to the sea-bed and of the sea-bed. With respect to "sea-bed" we are talking about flounders. They are on the sea-bed. As the Hon. Member said, we are not talking about drilling rights, mining rights, over-flights, or hampering of commercial traffic. We are dealing solely with the moving resources, the living resources of that area which already exist within the exclusive economic zone, together with marine scientific research which is involved in preservation and protection of the marine environment, another necessary power which the coastal states ought to be able to exercise in order to conserve, protect and manage any resource.
The rights and duties of other states within that area are also significant, and they appear under Article 58. In that exclusive economic zone all states enjoy, subject to relevant provisions, the freedoms referred to, and so on. In exercising those rights and performing those duties, however, those states, other than the coastal states, shall have due regard to the rights and duties of the coastal state, which concerns management, and shall comply with the laws and regulations adopted by the coastal state. We are considering, again, those laws and regulations relating to conservation.
In Article 61 one finds that among the management rights which the coastal state enjoys, are those of determining the allowable catch of the living resources in its exclusive economic zone. That is what we seek in this Bill, Mr. Speaker, to be extended those few hundred square miles to the nose and tail of the Georges Bank.
The territorial sea which is mentioned in the Bill is already included within that exclusive economic zone, so we can think of it not in terms of the technical definition of the territorial
Continental Shelf
sea, but rather as part of the exclusive economic zone which this Bill seeks to extend. To all intents and purposes, therefore, this Bill does no more than seek to extend jurisdiction over fisheries and fishermen for preservation over a few extra square miles or square kilometres which it now exercises within the exclusive economic zone, seaward beyond the edge of the 200 mile limit, so that it may conserve, protect and manage those stocks which flow into and out of, which move back and forth, in and out of the exclusive economic zone.
This is not an outrageous demand, Mr. Speaker, given the peculiarities of the continental shelf off the East Coast, and taking fish breeding grounds into account. What this Bill does not seek to do, and I believe this is most important, it does not seek to extend drilling rights. They are already there at a price. Nor does it seek to impede the passage of any commercial vessel or waterborne traffic, nor to hamper the passage of aircraft.
There is one matter that I would like to mention in conclusion. Perhaps we could somehow persuade Spain to accept a portion, anyway, of Article 64 of the Convention dealing with highly migratory species. Section 64 provides that the coastal state, and other states, whose nationals fish in the region for the highly migratory species-this is in Annex 1- shall co-operate directly and through appropriate international organizations with a view to ensuring conservation and promoting the objective of optimum utilization of such species throughout the region, both within and beyond the exclusive economic zone. In regions for which no appropriate international organization exists, the coastal state, and other states, whose nationals harvest these species in the region, shall co-operate to establish such an organization and participate in this work. That provision is now within the Law of the Sea Convention, Mr. Speaker. It may be difficult, but I do not think it is impossible, that Canada should be able to persuade the Government of Spain to abide by this Article even if it is unwilling to abide by the full text of the agreement.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to move that the subject matter, at least of this Bill, be referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry for further study.
